newsitem.title: FRANCE: Moslem rebels kill 14 people in Algeria.
newsitem.headline: Moslem rebels kill 14 people in Algeria.

text.p: Moslem guerrillas killed 14 people overnight in Tabainat village in Blida province, 50 km (30 miles) south of Algiers, Algerian security forces said on Monday.
The mass killing came on the fifth anniversary of the cancellation by Algeria's army-backed authorities of a general election which radical Islamists were poised to win.
The Algerian security forces said in a statement that the 14 people had been "assassinated in a cowardly way" -- the term they generally use for civilians killed by having their throats cut.

The statement, carried on the official Algerian news agency APS, blamed the killing on a "group of terrorists". Algerian authorities use this phrase to describe Moslem guerrillas fighting to overthrow the government since the January 12, 1992 cancellation of the election.

The overnight slaughter was the latest in a series of massacres carried out in darkness in villages in the past two months and a rash of bombings in Algiers and other cities in the North African country.
About 50 guerrillas stormed Douaouda village in the coastal province of Tipaza, 60 km (40 miles) west of Algiers, a week ago killing 18 villagers and wounding 18.
Sixteen villagers were killed in a similar rebel raid the same week in Ben Achour hamlet in the same province as the latest overnight killing.
Two car bombs six days ago killed 20 people in Algiers and Ain-Fakroun, a town 380 km (240 miles) east of the Algerian capital, after an Algerian guerrilla rebel threatened a wave of bombings.

The mass killings and bombings in which more than 250 people have died in the past two months prompted politicians and newspapers in Algeria to ridicule Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia over his repeated claims that his government had crushed the guerrillas.
"The government wants us to believe that the bombings were birds' singing," said moderate fundamenalist opposition leader Mahfoud Nahnah on Saturday.
Algeria's main secular opposition leader, Hocine Ait Ahmed, said on Friday the rulers had vested interests in lasting violence in the oil and gas producing country.
"The rulers want to reduce everything to an equation 'army versus fundamentalism'," said Ait Ahmed, adding that the killings were used as pretext to bar any real democratisation.

Algeria's banned Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) issued a statement to mark the anniversay of the cancellation of the general election in which it had taken a commanding lead, urging "soldiers and officers of the Algerian army to express their rejection of the policy of confronation and blood-letting".

Residents of Algiers said the rebel attack against Tabainat village, coming in the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan, weighed heavily on people. Many feared more raids and bombings as guerrillas reckon the holy month is a sacred time for what they call their 'holy war'.
About 60,000 people have died in Algeria's violence since January 1992.
